# Rye Sourdough

## Overview

This is the rye loaf I bake when I want something dense, sour and deeply coloured, built on 20% dark rye and 80% strong white flour at a 78% hydration mix. There is no autolyse step at all, because with rye in the dough a long rest just makes the whole thing slack and sticky; everything goes straight into the bowl and I get on with it. The rye brings a malty, almost earthy flavour and a tight, moist crumb that slices thin and toasts beautifully. The dough is softer than a white loaf and it never really gets a windowpane, so I judge it by feel: it should be tacky, hold a rough shape, and spring back slowly when I poke it. One fold is all I give it, since too much handling turns the dough into a paste. I shape it with a wet scraper rather than my hands, which keeps the surface smooth without fighting the stickiness. The bake starts covered and hot, then finishes uncovered and cooler, which sets the crust before it darkens too far. It keeps for three days wrapped in a tea towel, and it freezes very well sliced. The rye also makes the dough ferment faster than a white loaf would, so I watch the bowl rather than the clock.

## Method

I build the dough the night before with a spoonful of rye starter, water and the dark rye flour to make a loose rye sponge, and leave it covered on the counter until it smells sharply sour. In the morning I weigh 400 g of strong white flour and 100 g of dark rye into a big bowl, tip in 360 g of water and 200 g of active starter, and mix with a dough hook for three minutes, then rest ten minutes and mix in 10 g of salt with a splash more water. No autolyse here, everything is in the bowl from the start and the salt goes in after the first short mix. The dough should feel soft and slightly sticky.

I leave it in a warm spot for four hours, and at the halfway mark I do one fold, lifting the dough up and over itself from the four sides and tucking it back down. That single fold is enough to give the rye some structure without overworking it.

I tip the dough onto a wet board and shape it with a wet scraper, pushing the edges underneath and turning it until the top is tight and the base is sealed, then slide it into a floured banneton and cold proof it overnight.

In the morning I heat the oven and a covered pot to 240 C. I turn the loaf out onto baking paper, score it once down the middle, and bake it covered for 15 minutes at 240 C, then take the lid off and drop the heat to 220 C for 25 minutes until the crust is dark and the base sounds hollow. I cool it completely before cutting, because a warm rye loaf smears badly under the knife and the crumb firms up as it stands. The whole bake takes a little over two hours from turning the dough out to slicing it.

## Notes

Rye dough behaves differently from white dough in ways that catch people out, and the biggest one is that it never develops the same gluten. There is some gluten in rye but it is weaker, and the pentosans in the flour soak up a lot of water, which is why this dough is stickier than its hydration figure suggests. That is exactly why I skip the autolyse and why I only fold it once: extra time and handling make the dough looser rather than stronger, and there is no recovering from that. The wet scraper is the single most useful tool here, because a dry surface on such a sticky dough tears it and drags the top layer out of shape. I keep the hydration at 78% and no higher, since rye absorbs free water slowly and a wetter dough turns to soup after an hour. The dark rye gives the loaf its colour and its long sourness, and it also ferments faster than white flour, so I watch the bulk rather than trusting a clock. If the dough feels tight and dry after the salt, a small spoonful of water fixes it. A well-floured banneton and a quick confident turn are what get the loaf into the pot without losing its shape.

## Troubleshooting

If the loaf comes out gummy in the middle it needed longer in the uncovered stage, so give it another ten minutes and trust the hollow knock rather than the clock. If it spreads sideways in the pot the bulk went too long and the rye lost what little strength it had, so shorten the ferment next time. If the crust is pale the oven is running cool and I check the real temperature because mine reads about ten degrees low. If the dough is unmanageably sticky the hydration was too high for the flour, so hold back twenty grams of water until the mix comes together. If the crumb is tight and heavy the starter was sluggish, so refresh it a day ahead and wait for a proper dome before you bake. If the loaf tastes flat and sour without any sweetness, the bulk was too long and the sugars were used up, so cut an hour off the ferment next time.
